newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan fighters cut off Taleban forces, airbase.
newsitem.headline: Afghan fighters cut off Taleban forces, airbase.

text.p: Afghan fighters opposing the country's new purist Islamic Taleban rulers cut the main road north of Kabul and isolated its military airbase on Friday, killing several Taleban militia, witnesses and residents said.

Fighters apparently loyal to former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood shelled Bagram airbase, 50 km (30 miles) north of the capital. As night fell only the airbase appeared to remain in Taleban hands.

Travellers said a succession of guerrilla attacks from outlying villages had cut two roads leading from the north, where Taleban militia have been attacking Masood's valley base, harrying Taleban positions and vehicles on the roads.
Taleban fighters said the road north of Kabul had been cut some 15 km (10 miles) from the capital as far as Qarah Bagh another 20 km (12 miles) on.

About 20 local people arrived with a truck at Bagram village next to the airbase and used beds as stretchers to take away four Taleban corpses from an empty guardpost just south of the airstrip. The road was splattered with blood.
"We were told to take the bodies away because the Taleban can no longer get into the area," a villager said.
The attack on the airbase was matched by guerrilla ambushes and rocket attacks on Taleban positions along the road.
Just on from the main pass some 12 km (8 miles) north of Kabul, Taleban militia pounded positions on both sides of the road with rocket, artillery and anti-aircraft fire.
Fighters said that since morning local commanders in at least four villages had attacked the Taleban. At dusk, several tanks were moving out of the capital towards the fighting.
"Four districts have turned against us," one fighter said.

The road itself, the main artery between Kabul and the north through the Salang Pass in the Hindu Kush mountains, was virtually empty apart from Taleban-commandeered jeeps, tanks and families fleeing.
The attacks, apparently orchestrated by Masood, have hit the Taleban well behind their front line with Masood in the Panjsher valley and the Salang Pass.

The Taleban have their front line headquarters at Jabal-os-Siraj, a two-hour drive north of Kabul, at the mouth of the Salang. Territory controlled by Uzbek leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum begins in the pass.
The attacks near Kabul followed visits by Masood envoys urging groups to turn against the militia which drove him back to his Panjsher stronghold, local people said.

Witnesses said at least six shells landed inside the Bagram base perimeter during an hour-long attack, but it was not known whether there was any damage to the small number of Soviet-era MiG-23s the Taleban say they have there.

The Taleban sent up two helicopter gunships to fire rockets at the area from which the shells were being fired and they came under anti-aircraft fire but escaped unharmed. Damage to Masood's forces was not known.
Afghan-watchers in Kabul said Masood appeared to have reverted to the tactics he used against the Soviet army in the 1980s when Moscow backed a communist Afghan government.
His ethnic Tajiks survived a series of assaults on the Panjsher and often struck back in the Salang Pass. Then they would stage hit-and-run raids in the Soviet rear.
The largely ethnic Pushtun Taleban launched an assault on the gorge that leads into the Panjsher last Saturday. After four days of fighting they had penetrated barely 500 yards (metres).
On Tuesday, Masood commander Basir Solangi struck suddenly in the Salang, cutting off a large body of Taleban and inflicting heavy casualties, witnesses said.
The attack forced the Taleban to break off their bid on the Panjsher and switch men to the new front as well as call up heavy reinforcements from Kabul.
